THE WARRINGTON TRADES EXHIBITION. EMPIE HALAL 141/A.ERI NOTO N. October 28th to November 14th.

The Managers of the Empire Hall beg to intimate to Manufacturers, Merchants and Retailers, that it is their intention to organise a huge Trades Exhibition in the above Hall, which is the largest In Warrington and ranks as one of the finest in Lancashire. " Empire Hail" has a floor area without impediment or column of 18,000 square feet and possesses the most improved conveniences, having a fine Lounge Bandstand, Offices, Cloak Rooms and Electric Fitments so tiecessary for an ideal Exhibition, The Musical engagements are unique and Include the celebrated Verona Ladies' Orchestra, as well as local singers and entertainers both Amateur and Professional. In addition many Side Shows of an amusing and pleasing nature have been secured to ensure a varied and complete change of Program each day during the full period of the Exhibition.

The whole arrangements surpass anything that has been previously attempted in Warrington. The Exhibition will afford the leading retail hoases a long-wished-for opportunity of availing themselves of this unequalled form of publicity. For Plans and full particulars apply to Messrs SMITH & TURTON, Crampton's Chambers, Bridge Street, Warrington.
W V. TURTON, Secretary. Tlp.•

div.head: CORONATION DISPUTE.
div.p: CORONATION DISPUTE.
THE COUNCIL AND THE TEACHERS.
Lively Scene

The attitude of the teachers of Warrington with regard to the Coronation festivities ,'orrned the subject .hf a lively debate at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tumidity evening. The discussion arose on the minuteo of the General Purposes Committee hhich contained a reference to the arrangements for the Coronstioo celebrations and I the presentation of a loyal address to his Majesty the The MA von, in moving the adoption of the winner, said be wished to refer to an important subject and that was the relationship which existed between the Corona- tion Committee end the head teachers of Warrington. The Council would have noticed what had been mid and what he looked upon es the false impressi n which had been given to the public. div.p: WARRINGTON CHAPTERS. ).‘,-,•'‘..... ^.-.,,,,,V,,zw•,..,NeAi,...#%e4.
COLONEL BLOOD. The Man Who Stole the Royal Regalia.
His Ties with Warrington.

Most visitors to London have scaled the steps of the Beauchamp Tower and peered between the bars upon the Royal crown and sceptre, and few folks, we imagine, have grudged the modest sixpence which buys the Privilege of seeing the most costly things that common mortals are ever likely to look upon. Collected by monarchs through centuries the fine jewels sparkle tantalizingly behind the bars and the famous red ruby blazes in the front of the crown as it did long centuries back upon the field of Agincourt. Mention of the Royal Regalia inevitably brings the reminder of Colonel Blood, and admiration of the jewels is often diverted just a little by the memory of the fine audacity of the man who once removed them from the Tower. "I guess I don't know which to admirei" said an American visitor to the Tower of London "the Regalia, or the colossal cheek of the man who stole it, and then managed to get a pension as his punish- ment." This comment hits off the facts of the case. Colonel Blood stole the crown, orb and sceptre after nearly murdering the warder and his only punishment from King Charles 11. was a pension of £5OO a year and ten years of Royal favour. This magnificent scoundrel, Colonel Blood, had many ties with Warrington of which we hope to tell some other day. In the present chapter, with reminders of the Coronation so thickly spread around us, it may be appropriate to tell how the precious Royal Regalia was once dragged ignominously from the Tower. It was not until the year 1670 that the public were allowed to see the Crown jewels. In that year Sir Gilbert Talbot was keeper of the Tower of London and, as resident keeper, one Talbot Edwards lived in chambers near to the Regalia room. A small fee was charged for admission, and among those who early called to gratify curiosity was Thomas Blood an adventurer who had come through the Civil War, and who ought long before before to have been honoured with a Tyburn Gibbet.

COLONEL -BLOOD'S MARRIAGE AT NEWCHURCIL Blood was the son of an Irish blacksmith and inherited a fine dark handsome face and a gift of specious and pleasing eloquence. Through a friendship formed in Cromwell's army he came to know Thomas Holcroft of Culcheth and successfully made love to Maria Holcroft his eldest sister. The family mistitusted Thomas Blood notwithstanding his fine exterior,and when upon a day in the middle of the civil wars the wedding was celebrated at Newchurch it was only a small party that celebrated the events at Holcroft Hall. .
----- The church register records the events in Latin.

Thomas Blood gene et Maria Holm oft mats imnnio eopulati viceasimo primo die Junui nano domi 11151). It has another event to record in the following year. Thomas Una Thome', 8100 lan haptizatus 311 too Martii anon donii 105/.

It was twenty years after the birth of Thomas Blood the younger that he,as a young man, was drawn into the plot which his father was carefully preparing. Those twenty years had seen Colonel Blood passing through countless adventures with Covenanters and Fifth Monarchy Men and engaged in a most reckless and audacious attempt to seize and summarily hang the Duke of Ormond. He would have been infamous had he never set eyes on the crown jewels, but this crowning act of hazard has lived in the public mind, and will make him famous for ever.
THE PLOT TO 'STEAL THE REGALIA.

In April 1671 Colonel Blood, disguised as a minister, visited the Tower in company with a lady whom he alleged was his wife. This however, was not Maria Holcroft, for she lay ill at the time at Holcroft Hall. The long ministerial gown concealed a club and had ample pockets and it was the design of Blood to disable the warder and get possession of his keys. The lady fainted at an opportune moment, but the warder tdid not bend over her as had been expected. Instead he called his wife who took the lady into her care.
PLOT THE SECOND.

The failure of the first plot opened the way to a second. It gave opportunity to visit the Tower on the pretence of bringing presents and expressing gratitude. This was done by the Colonel and his accomplice and the friendship prospered. The gratitude of the couple seemed endless and Blood finally crowned his display of appreciation by say- ing that he was sure he could find a wonderful n:atch for the warder's daughter. He declared that he had a young nephew worth two to three hundred pounds a year whom he would bring in the hope of them falling in love. This " nephew ' was the son born and christened at Newchurch twenty years before and on the appointed day at seven in the morning Blood and three friends appeared at the jewel house. Talbot Edwards was up to receive them, but his daughter thought it hardly modest to descend so quickly and sent down her maid as spy. The maid brought a favourable report of the young man and Miss Edwards decided to come down only when called. In the meantime the warder was chatting with " Parson " Blood little suspecting what lay under his gown, and the plotter was innocently suggesting that his friends had not seen the jewels and might perhaps be allowed to do so whilst they waited for his wife.

They had no sooner entered the chamber than a cloak was thrown over the old man's head and a gag pushed into his mouth. He cried aloud, in spite of their threats, until knocked down by a mallet and even then raised the best alarm he could until stabbed in the stomach and clubbed into silence. Regarding him as dead the plotters secured his keys and promptly packed the orb. Blood placed the crown under his cloak and his friends were just about to We the sceptre in two in order that it might be placed in a bag. .

At this critical moment an entirely unsuspected incident brought confusion. The details are carefully told by Bayley in his " History of the Tower of London •' and we borrow from him the details of this part of the exciting story.

div.head: CHASE.
div.p: THE CHASE.

"A son of Mr. Edwards, had been in Flanders with Sir John Talbot, and on his landing in England had obtainei leave to come away. He happened to arrive at this moment, and on coming to the door the person that stood sentinel asked with whom he would speak, to which he answerel that he belonged to the house; and, perceiving the person to be a stranger, told him that if

he had any business with. his father that he would acquaint him with it, and so hastened upstairs to salute his friends. This unex- pected accident spread confusion amongst the party, and they instantly decamped with the crown and orb, leaving the sceptre yet unfiled "

- ..... -- The aged keeper now raised himself upon his legs, forced the gag from his mouth, and cried '' Treason! Murder" which being heard by his daughter, who was, perhaps, anxiously expecting other sounds.ran out and reiterated the cry. The alarm now became general, and young Edwards and his brother-in-law, Captain Beckman, ran after the conspirators. A warder put him- self in a position to stop; but Blood dis- charged a pistol at him, and he fell, although I unhurt. The thieves proceeded safely to the next guard, where one Sill, who had been a soldier under Cromwell, stood sentinel; but he offered no opposition, and they accord- ingly passed the drawbridge. Horses were waiting for them at St. Catherine's gate, and as they ran that way along tto Tower wharf, they themselves cried out "Stop the rogues" • by which they passed on unsuspected till Captain Beckman overtook them. At his head Blood fired another pistol, but missed him, and was seized. Under the cloak of this daring villain was found the crown, and, although he saw himself a prisoner, he had yet the impudence to struggle for his prey; and when it was finally wrested from him, said, _
"It was a gallant attempt, however, unsuccessful; it was for a crown."

_ Parrot, who had formerly served under General Harrison, was also taken ; but Hunt, Blood's son-in-law, reached his horse and rode off, as did two other of the thieves; but he was soon afterwards stopped, and likewise committed to custody.

In this struggle and confusion the great pearl, a large diamond, and s.weral smaller stones were lost from the crown; but the two former and some of the latter were after- wards found, and restored ; and the Ballas ruby, broken off the sceptre, being found in Parrot's pocket, nothing considerable was eventually missing.
As soon as the prisoners were secured, young Edwards hastened to Sir Gilbert

„ Talbot, who was then master and treasurer of the Jewel-house, and gave him an account of the transaction Sir Gilbert instantly went to the King and acquainted him with it ; and his majesty commanded him to proceed forthwith to the Tower, to see how matters stood; to take the examination of Blood, and the others; and to return and report it to him. Sir Gilbert accordingly went; but the King in the meantime was persuaded by some about him to hear the examination himself, and the prisoners were in consequence sent for to Whitehall.

KING CHARLES MEETS COLONEL BLOOD. What followed is one of the standing puzzles of history. King Charles not only pardoned the man who had stolen his crown but gave him a pension of £5OO a year and a . .

place. in his Court at Whitehall. 'So extra- o- dinary was the climax that the suggestion was made and widely believed that Charles knew of the robbery beforehand and had arranged to share the proceeds of it. But before accepting any such alarming , conclusion it is well to remember (as our
puzzled historians have failed to do) that the meeting between the King and Colonel Blood was a meeting between one of the meekest and one of the most audacious of men.
Blood told the King that the country swarmed with his enemies; that on more

than one occasion he himself had pointed his carbine to shoot him; that once he had lain in the rushes by the Thames at Gravesend to shoot the King as he passed in his barge but that overawed by the King's majesty of person he had not dared to pull the trigger . .

and that lie had cried out in his awe to the rest to desist fire. He told him, too, that hundreds were hound by an oath as enemies , of the King and that should one of the num- ber be put to death the King's life would be forfeit. Moreover, said Blood, an act of

clemency would be regarded With favour, would "oblige the hearts of many," and show to the King's enemies that he was not the monster he was painted. There was probably not a word of truth in the statement, but it seems to have told heavily upon the debauched monarch. "Art thou craving pardon, then?" said Charles. "Only that the pardon may spare His Majesty's neck," said Blood. History surely records no parallel to such colossal impudence, and history tells of nothing so successful. For decency's sake Charles sent the offenders to the Tower, but in a few days Blood got a letter, a pardon, a pension and the restoration of his estates in Ireland which he had lost during the war. Talbot Edwards recovered from his wound and as the reward fora life offered in defence of the Crown was granted £2OO. His son was granted £lOO, but neither sum was ever paid, and they sold the grant for half its value to someone who seemed able to extract it from the Treasury. Small wonder that England grew tired of the Stewarts. THE END AND AFTERWARDS.

Colonel Blood moved in Court Society for nearly ten years. Then, having libelled the Duke of Buckingham,a law suit went against him and he was ordered to pay £lO,OOO. This seems to have broken his heart and he I died on August 24th, 1680. But the people could not believe that a man like Colonel Blood would die so easily. He had shed so much innocent blood, and gone through so much violence that the popular mind refused to think that he would ever die upon his bed. The rumour spread that he was still alive. So persistent was the statement that official notice was taken of
it,and the Coroner summoned a jury and had the body exhumed. Identification was difficult but the thumbs had in life been of abnormal size and by these identity was established.
In the fashion of the times the poets wrote of his exploits so soon as he was safely underground, and one very drastic "Eligie I was published as a leaflet. It began:

Thank ye kind Fates for your last favour shown, Of abiding Blood who lately stole the crown. and ended with a suggested epitaph : Here lire the Man who boldly hath von through More \litanies than ever England knew And here to any friend he had was true, Here let him then by all unpittied lye And let's Re j,,yce his time was come to Dye.

It may be added as of local interest that both of Colonel Blood's confederafies on the morning of May 9th 1671 were familiar with the streets of Warrington. One was his son-in-law, a young man from Culcheth, named Hunt, and the other was Parrot (possibly a nick-name) who had served with Colonel Harrison in the wars when Warring- ton was the sphere of his operations. A.M.

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, NP. SOME NEEDED AMENDMENTS TO THE INSURANCE BILL.

The Whitsuntide Conferences of the Friendly Societies have on the whole given a fairly favourable reception to the Insurance Bill. It would have been strange if it had been otherwise, for the Bill has been drafted with the fear of the Friendly Societies ever before the eye of the draftsman. The Con- ferences have suggested certain amendments most of which are very reasonable and desirable. If ever there was a Bill which needed drastic amendment in detail it is this Bill. Nothing in ccipnection with the discussions upon it has been more surpris- ing than the way in which the Trade Unions and the Labour Party have not merely accepted but welcomed and embraced the contributory basis of the scheme. These bodies appear to have forgotten the reason for their existence, which is to get for the workers that share of the national wealth of which they are at present unjustly deprived. That object is never going to be attained by putting the cost of carrying out reforms upon the wage-earners themselves, which is what this Insurance Bill does to a very great extent. It has for years been a platitude on Labour and Trade Union plat- forms to declare that the responsibility for dealing with unemployment and poverty wan a national obligation, and every scheme they have put forward to deal with these matters has been based on the principle that the cost must be recovered from the unearned wealth of the rich. .

Now all this appears to be forgotten, and a proposal which makes the workers them- selves responsible for finding most of the money to pay for treating sickness and unemployment socially is received with approval and elmmendation, and indeed is justified from the Labour benches of the House of Commons on the same grounds, and in almost t. • same phrases as those Mr. John Burns h—s used whenever he has been opposing some Labour proposal, namely that nothi, • t b .w.e to undermine the self-re!' ~ : thrift ..f the workers ! In practice a. ~ave long since abandoned the idea that self-help ceases to be self help when it is exercised through the collective .o-operation of the whole body of citizens known as the State. These arguments about destroying individual responsibility were used when it was proposed to starts national Education System, but who dare now main- tain that there is a weaker sense of parental responsibility now than when a man was allowed to neglect to give his children any schooling at all. THE CONTRIBUTORY BASIS.

The few of us who are opposed to the principle of a contributory scheme were not allowed to speak in the Second Reading debate There evidently was a desire that no dis- cordant note should mar the chorus of fulsome adulation which was sentup in praise of the Bill. But it will be difficult to prevent differences from expressing themselves in the Committee stage, and, unless the Govern- ment closure 911 important amendments as they did on the Old Age l'ensions Bill, the question of a non-contributory scheme will be raised. This is the most important of the amendments which can be moved. It is hardly likely to carry, for if it did it would mean the withdrawal of the Bill and sub- stitution of one entirely reconstructed. But apart from such a radical amend- ment as that,there are many very important ones which must be pressed. First of all comes the question of the treatment of women under the Bill. The Chancellor has I announced that it is intended to keep the women in a separate class and to make them self-supporting. This is not fair. If women, owing to the accident of their sex, are more liable to sickness than men, that is not a reason why they should be asked to bear the additional burden, but it is a strong reason why men should take it up and bear . it, for the additional sickness to which women are liable is due to causes in which all society is interested. The treatment of women who marry is not satisfactory under the Bill as it stands at present. It is all very well for the Chan- cellor to instruct his clerks to write letters to the Press pointing out that there is no for- feiture of premiums in the cases where a woman who has been an insured worker marries and thus ceases to be entitled to benefits, but the fact is that she never does resume the enjoyment of the funds she has contributed unless she survives her husband and then goes back to work. In all other eases, which will be the majority, she forfeits all the premiums which have been deducted fr.= her wages. It should be possible to get an amendment in Committee by which the money she has paid could be invested for her in the Post Office, and be made with- drawable at her request. The Conference of Oddfellows drew atten- tion to one very indefensible provision in the Bill, which deals with the case of the man who is doubly insured. The amount a man can draw from the State Insurance must not exceed two-thirds of his wage, and if he is drawing sick pay from other sources equal to his ordinary wages then he is not to be allowed any State benefit. This and many other provisions in the Bill seem to have been framed with the fear of the malingerer in mind. The hypothetical individual seems to have been haunting Mr. Lloyd George all the time he has been framing the Bill. There is no justification for depriving a man of the full sum for which he is insured because the total happens to be equal to or to exceed his ordinary wages. OTHER POINTS ABOUT WOMEN.

The Maternity Benefit is in a very unsatis- factory way at present. It is a sum of 308., but this has not to be paid in money to the husband or wife, but to be given in kind by the approved society or the Health Com- mittee. This is an offensive way of doing the thing. It suggests that the insured persons are not fit to be trusted with a sum of 305., but it must be doled out to them like soup or blankets from a charity. The Sick- ness Benefit is not to be paid to an insured woman in addition to Maternity Benefit, so that in such cases there is no maternity grant at all in reality. An attempt will be I made in Committee to secure that the insured woman shall be entitled to receive the sick- ness allowance at such times as well as the maternity benefit. The right of women to be represented on the governing bodies which are to be set up under the Bill is in no way safeguarded. It is very necessary that women should be represented, as they will account for about five million insured persons, and their advice and experience in matters of sickness etc. will be very useful. The Bill does not permit those who are at present suffering from permanent disable- ment to come within the operation of the measure. A person who becomes perman- ently disabled within two years of the passing of the Act, though he may have con-

tributed to the fund all that time, will not be entitled to the permanent grant of ss, a a week, but on the contrary, as the Bill now stands he will be cast adrift after exhausting the 26 weeks' sickness payments. This is,a detail of the Bill which needs amendment. The permanently disabled must be a charge upon somebody, and the State is the hack. best able to carry them. The blind, too, are not able to come on the ,permanent (Usable- ment fund, and, unles Alan amendment be inserted in the Bill they will be driven to become Post Office contributors as the Friendly Societies will have the right to reject them. Blindness, like age, should be one of OA grounds which do not entitle Qiie society to reject an applicant. • WHION OUT OF WORK.

One of the most iMportant things in the oy Bill is the question of tie pdymentiif contri- butions to the Sick ss Fund when the insured person istat work. As the thing stands at present, the conjributions m sp,not be paid at such times, but, if nokarrears will accrue with all the accompanying penalties or reduced benefits. But the worst thing about this matter is, that when out of work the workman is to be re,ponsible not only for his own premiums but for those of the employer, too. This plan cannot "-poseibly,. work, and it ought not to work. When a F man is involuntarily out of employment he ought not to be charged with paymente at all. The State ought to assume responsi- bility at such times. When the insured person is sick no payments are to be made, nor will arrears accrue. The same thing should apply to unemployment.

div.head: VERY OLD.
div.p: THE VERY OLD.

The treatMeni.-of.pei;Ons'iiTt-Ween the ages 65 and 70 is very hard. They are left out in the cold altogether. They are too old for the Sickness Insurance and they are too young for the Old Age Pension. It is true that sickness increases rapidly after 65 and the cost of including these people in the scheme !might have made it very expensive, but if they cannot be provided for in one way they should in another, and the Pension age ought to he reduced to 65. At 70 years of age an insured person must conic out of the Insurance scheme. He may have paid for a great many years and drawn no benefits, but when he arrives at the age of 70 he must forfeit all his premium paid to the fund, and presumably conic on the Old Age pension list. He is not even to have a claim to medical relief. This is most unfair. If he is not to receive both pension and sick pay at the same time he surely should be entitled to medical relief. He ought to have something for all the money he has paid. _

These are only a few of the amendments of an important character which should be made in the Bill. Although I believe the basis of the Bill, that is its contributory character, is wrong, there are many good features in the Bill which entitles it to support. It is a big experiment, and a fe'W years of the working of it will give that experience we do not possess at present, and which will enable a better measure to be framed.

div.head: CHILDREN'S CORNER, i Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
div.p: CHILDREN'S CORNER, i Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
.\ It( )UT CORONATIONS AND CROWNS
hie of my constant readers has copied for me a poem which says in words what a good many of us must have been thinking. It iv called "Coronation Everything."
There are Coronation kittens, and Coronation eats, Coronation mitten., and I%,ronation mate
Coronation " pinnies " and Coronation pins Coronation fish. with Coronation fins ;

Coronation VBS., C01'0486011 clocks, Coronation 4 eltings. and Coronation socks ; Cto, nation ' hankies," Coronation tiea, Cortmation hooka to make you Coronation wise We are Corooltion jolly, Coronation glad,

And before the mho; imover we'll be Coronation mad. There is a danger of getting Coronation mad and I did not think I would say any- thing about it, but as this is a special Coronation number it would look very bad indeed if I did not. Suppose then I tell you that in old Rome and Greece they used to have a lot more 'Aironations than we have. Indeed every- body had the chance to earn a Corona- tion it they did anything that was thought of one. In Athens, in her best days, they used to give crowns of gold to anyone who did good public service and you have read how all the young men used to strive in;the athletic festivals to win a crown of laurels and parsley. In the Roman army there were four kinds of crowns that a man might earn. There was what was called "Corona Muralis " (corona is Latin for crown) which was given to the soldier who first scaled the walls of a besieged city. There was also the "Corona Vallaris" given to the one who first forced an entrench- ment, and the "Corona Obsidionalis" for the general who relieved a city from siege. For sea fighters there wan the "Corona Navalis" which was decorated with little figures of the prows of ships given to the one who dis- tinguished himself at sea. And all these crowns were put on at Coronation festivals after the wars were over.

I If crowns are to be symbols of honour the old Greek plan of giving them to all who earned them strikes one as being very good. They did not conic down from father to son like our own ducal coronets but were given to those considered worthy and the Greeks were wiser than the Romans, for they valued services done to the State. If this custom were common amongst us in our day we should have some capital Coronations. We should see General Booth driving up to Westminster Abbey (or somewhere else) in his motor car to get crowned, and Dr. Bernardo would have had to go long since, and to would Florence Nightingale and the late Earl Shaftesbury. Marconi would get a crown for wireless telegraphs and Lloyd George for giving Old Age Pensions. And as every Coronation would mean a holiday from school it would be very jolly indeed. And some statesman some day would abolish home lessons for boys and girls, and we would crown him for that, and the holiday that came for that would be the jolliest of all. We shall really have to all try to get the great custom brought back again.

div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
(By Redcap.)
THE DUST BATH.

One only needs to observe how readily fowls mesh ton duet-bath to realize its importance. When given their liberty they soon makes bath for themselves ; but when otherwise kept in c!cse confinement it is absolutely es-ential for their cornrow to rovide :hem with a du-t bath. This can easily be dire by making a box about toe foot deep; fill it with dry ashes or road dust, and add to thiso good handful of powdered sulphur. During the summer months when the weather is warm insert vermin propagate rapidly ao.I the use of the bath is the only and natural process that • hen has of ridding herself of these pests ; therefore it is essential that you should provide the stock with a dust bath. Always place it where the sun can play upon it v this means ;t is kept dry.
ETIII

There is always something to be learn,' whilst following the pursuits of the poultry indu.try. The follow') g is an extract from a correspondent in the • Poultty World," and One which I feel sure will be of interest and profit to many. It is a new way of ' providing chickens with intact life. Ile vats;—" For the backyarder whose fowls cannot get the insects that fools pi, in crn runs a trip good plan is to get a large Maser at and fill it with sandy soil, first mixing in some fine sugar. Do not put in any crocks. Place this whe:e y.iu see any ante, and put a board /ir cloth over it. Leave for about font, teen dam thou lift up and empty in chicken run. It will be found full of ants and ants' eggs, and the chickens naturally have a hoe time." No doubt this is a very good hint lint some of my readers may ask what shall I do if I can fo.cl no ants? lAt me help you The earth abounds with insect life of many varieties, and the foregoing is undoubtedly a good plan for at trading theta. line not necessary that you should attract ants only. Almost all of the small. creeping insects are goof for chickens, ao you see if you did not necessarily attract ants, you would certainly attract others. The plan might be further adopted by making a mixtare of soil and animal food of some deacri)ition noun fi, attract flies. 'Fake a piece of flesh meat and place it in the chicken run, securely cover the same with a piece of sacking (so that the chickens could not devour it) and as the flies are attracted to the nmst, the efikka find rare sport and exercise in jumping at them. All these !title hints tend to make the life of a chick contented and happy, and we all know that contentment is the first aid to a robust life.

, I have been told that rhubarb haves are a good thing for poultry. I have never tried them, hut intend doing no. I should recommend you, when experimentirg, to boil them and chop them up finoly and min it the soft food. lam told that fowls which have 'wen fed as above have thrived wonderfully, If this is oxrect it will be worth knowing, because at this season of the year it is not a difficult matter to get rhubarb loaves i shundat.ce.
IIIEAO A%l Ink.

In last week's roams! promised to tell yon of the wonderful recovery of fowl which was fed on the above diet. One of my readers who is a keen student of poultry tried the experiment. Ile had a black Long- shim hen sitting out a bstelt of eggs. She gradually wasted until she was no weak that it was impossible for her to generate any heat. Consequently my friend took her from the ne.t and began to feed her generously on bleed and milk. Ile first soaked the bread in water. strained it and then soaked it in milk. continned feeding with the addition of well stewed groats. After a week under this treatinent she laid oo egg. She continued to lay for eleven days Then she rr sted for three days and commenced laying again. She in now the pin tore of perf.ct health, and promises to continue filling the egg basket. Tide ins wonderful recovery, for the hen was so weak that she had to be fed by hand. It only goes to prove that inilk is a wonderful and natural stimulant. thy those who know its value it in greatly used, especially when rearing prize stock.

It is strange how—after much writing on the sub- ject of feeding - people continue to use maize almost an the staple diet. In I[4 place and judicious'y given, it ins good food. But there is no food which, when given indiscriminately, disorganises the liver so much. It is far too stimulating and heat-pr,ducing. unleis the fowls have a free range and plenty of green food to c,..tinteract the tercets. Maize does not cause liver disease, but when the liver becomes dis- organised by too much stimulating food, it easily hills a prey to disease. Hens in confined runs should never lie given maize, except very occasionallly in very cold weather. On the other hand fowls which, have their liteity and have access to a natural diet can be given maize at times with advantage,especiall7 if they are in an exposed position, but even then it ishould be avoided in hot weather. Always use your ',en judgment, nod use it in accordance with prevail- ing circumstances.

1111, 111-1,111.E.0 "Itllllll There are PO many different breeds and varieties of Poultry th.t the amateur is bewildered when attempt- ing to decide chat to go in for. If you are taking up poultry for a hobby and not as a business or for exhibilion purposes, it would be as well to gain for a good all-round bread. A pen of pure bred fowls alweys looks better than a pen of mongrels. There- fore I should always recommend you to get a pen of pure bred fowhi of a good. laying strain. In their uniformity of eoLur and sue they look better, they are more taking to the eye, and your neighbours remark "If a nice lot of fowls fir Jcnes keeps,- whil-t a pen of mongrels never attract either the eye Cr the purse. What then shall we say are a good amateor's fowl ? It will not he bat space if I name a few of the best breeds for the amateur to take up.

These are very nice looking fowls, easy t, rear, very docile, ant extremely us-lot. The Minorca Coo is a good amateurs fowl, especially in town iuns as they do not show the dirt like light-coloured fcwfs do. The Black Leghorn and the Ancona serve the same purpose. The light-coloured varieties are heat kept on glass rune, and when they ern be kept clean they look very taking indeed. The following varieties still serve the purpose very well —Buff Orpington, While Wyandove, Faveroile, White Legliorns. Bun Leghorn, and Brown Leghorn. These are all extremely useful fowls and at the same dine make an ideal picture when kept on a good grass ran !

div.head: Bowling Notes. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT BOWLING
div.p: Bowling Notes. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT BOWLING
- LEAGUE AFFILIATED TO THE COUNTY.

At a Meeting ' of the and District League held at the Midland Hotel on Monday evening it was resolved by a good majority that they affiliate them- selves to the Lancashire County Association. This decision was arrived at after an explanatory and 1 persuasive speech by Mr. Coombs (president of the County). Their wise conclusion trill enable the members of the League to take part in all competitions promoted by the County Assec anon and also partial- pate in the Works Bowling Association cotopetitioLs, providing, of couree, they are members ef the works clubs. Really, it is a pity that Mr. Coombs was not at the general meeting in Match when this matter waa discussed, becansa I feel sure that had his views been considered thoroughly they would have come to a decision contrary to what they did then. For the sake of no miaunderstandings I might mention that on no ace tint may any member who has been affiliated to the Loncashire County Aseociation and has played in the Blackpool sweep, engage in any competition pro- moted by the Asseciation bectmae he has infringed the amateur status.

div.head: PREVALENCE OF ADDERS.
div.p: THE PREVALENCE OF ADDERS.

One of the signs of the exceedingly hot and arid condition. of the ep ring lathe unusual number of adders that have been met with in all pliers of thoir mewl. Not only •0, but it appears that their bite bas been more than normally v.uomous. As an rule • dog that is bitten 1.5 an adder suffers severely from " smelled head "foe several days, bnt by the end of a week or no is all right again. Thin 5 ear we Lave beard of dogs being affected for a good deal longer, and in one case, , that of a apaniel which eas in perfect health when hitten, death resulted. This is quite nominal, and it is likely that aft... long spill of hot, dry weather the vital energies of these snakes are et their highest points, so that their poison glands are very fully charged and their bite. tbeiefore more virulent than usual. It follows that special attention shoold be given at tech times to any patient, human or canine, that hes been bitten by as adder, and though some people have, no doubt, an absurd fear of anikl‘PF, still it is only prudent to" go delicately " where •dders are known to be.—" Country Life."

Several of the party joined the boat immediately, and ventured through the three...tuarter mile tunnel between Preston Brook and Hutton, but the remainder pr. ferret] to walk over the top and -pined the boat at the Dutton end Very noon the camera shottera were heard clicking, ildicating that the scenery along the hanks of the canal was pleaaing the eyes of the members All along one con.insous panorama unfolded with many fine view, of the Weaver Valley presenting thetuselven an the trees opened flirt io the bank. We have previously 1 WARRINGTON'S taken the liberty of CHOICE. quoting from the

" Huddersfield Daily Examiner" some very outspoken opinions on the present member for Warrington, and we are interested to note that his excursions in the political field are still watched with considerable closeness by our Yorkshire contemporary. Mr. Harold Smith's speech atAsh ton- in- Makerfield last Saturday has evoked the following critical and damaging analysis of his attitude to men and matters of the day: Time and responsibility have had no effect on Mr. HAROLD SMITH. It was hoped that the errors of judgment and taste which he displayed in his Huddersfield campaign were only those of youth, the outcome of a perhaps natural desire to equal a successful brother to whose solecisms he was perhaps excusably blinded. Now, however, that Warrington— less careful and less wise than Huddersfield—has committed her political reputation into his hands he shows no sign of improvement in the temper of his utterances or of change in the innate character of the spirit which prompts them. Thus, speaking at Ashton-in-Makerfield, on Saturday last, he chose to say of the members of the Government that they had duped the country for the sake of the personal gains they could get out of politics. The working-classes were becoming alive to the fact that they had been duped by the Free Traders, "by those who placed party first and the Empire second, who cared more for their own salaries" than for Imperial interests. The only comment upon assertions of this kind is that they are worthy of the men who make them, and write them down as unfit for responsible position and unworthy of ordinarily courteous reply. It is amazing that the party which professes to be the party of British gentlemen should have room for such speakers amongst its representative men.

Declining to answer Mr. H. SMITH in kind, we will deal with him as an honourable English gentleman whose arguments deserve to be carefully weighed and dealt with according to their intrinsic quality. He remarked, with a characteristic use of the superlative, that it was impossible to over- estimate the importance of the proposed arrangement between Canada and the United States. Accepting Mr. SMITH'S exaggeration as a way of stating that very great import- ance attaches to the proposed agreement we have to point out that the importance lies in the impetus which such a movementtowards free exchange between two rich neighbour- ing territories will give to the general move- ment towards Free Trade. How little Mr. HAROLD SMITH knows of the true character of the relations between the Mother Country and the daughter States was revealed in his declaration that "if we allowed one part of the Empire to have better terms than another in a foreign market we should allow a thing most injurious to British trade and British workmen." The leaders of the Tory party, when the matter was before the House of Commons, were very chary of meeting the challenge to say if they were prepared to affirm that the Government ought to inter- fere with the right of a self-governing colony to decide its own affairs. The man who represents the political intelligence of War-1 rington has no hesitation in accusing the Government of thinking of their owo salaries when they refuse to enter upon another quarrel such as that which lost us the great colony of the United States. Having thus proclaimed his readiness to repeat the folly which lost us the brightest jewel of the British crown, Mr. HAROLD SMITH made an appeal that was indeed extra- ordinary in the light of what he had said about Liberal statesmen. He asked his hearers, not for the sake of their country, but for the money that might be made out of it, to take up the cause of what is still 'called Tariff Reform. "He appealed to the men of Lancashire," says the Unionist paper upon whose report our comments are based, "not through patriotism, but from a business point of view, to help to bring about the adoption of the great policy which, even if it did not stop the rot in the export trade, would build up something for future genera- tions by securing markets by preferential tariffs." That a man who degrades contro- versy by attributing to his opponents the base

motive of desiring salaries before the welfare of the Empire, should recommend Tariff Reform, not for the country's sake, but because it is good business, is surely evidence that Mr. HAROLD SMITH'S patriotism is of the some quality as his " gentilesse." When, however, he talks of stopping the rot in exports, it is necessary to ask him to give the figures of exports for any number of years back he cares to take and to show where the rot has taken place. In the absence I of such proof, it is possible only to conclude that this member of Parliament who makes such base but characteristic insinua- tions about the motives of his opponents is himself not above attempting to mislead his audiences on a matter of fact which is of vital importance in the discussion of the question at issue. Warrington may be proud of her choice. But a little more self-revela- tion of her member—who apparently desires tocopy his elder brother's methods without the characteristics which give those methods a semblance of brilliance and effectiveness— will, we fear, considerably chasten her pride.
There will be no lack

THE CORONATION, of hearty loyal senti- ment in Warrington on Thursday next when the coronation of His Gracious Majesty King George V. will be celebrated, and however adequate or inadequate the available means of expressing that sentiment, Warrington people will in their heart of hearts be fervently wishing a long and happy reign to the worthy successor of theßoyal and revered sovereign who passed away so suddenly a little more than twelve months ago and left behind him memories which will long remain fragrant and green. It is unquestionably a matter for regret tl -t on this forthcoming festive occasion, toe arrangements locally for celebrating the accession of a king fall considerably behind what has previously been the standard in Warrington and what is being done else- where. We are not advocates of what is euphemistically termed " making a splash" on these occasions, and in endeavouring to carry out their celebrations on reasonably 11 economical lines the Coronation Committee adopted a policy which will doubtless appeal to the inhabitants of a heavily-rated town.' But there are certain things which should not under any circumstances be omitted from the programme of such a memorable event, and the first of these is unquestionably a " treat " for the children which will fix the day in their minds and endow it with the full significance which it should have for every inhabitant, young or old, of these islands. Now the fact remains, and it is rather a sad one, that through various difficulties which we do not propose to enumerate—but which we think might have been obviated by more tactful methods—the children of Warrington are to be left to celebrate the day in their own unguided way. There are no festivities for them to take a part in, and nothing but a civic procession to impress upon their young minds the fact that a new King has come to the throne of this great Kingdom. Things might have been different and better in so many respects. Even the religious significance of the event has been largely lost sight of, and the unhappy internecine dispute between the municipal authorities and the teachers makes a blot on the page of Warrington's history which only time will hide, and for which only posterity can apportion the blame.

The Bishop of Chester , AN EPISCOPAL is not that rara aria, a MANIFESTO. Liberal prelate. Con- sequently his letter to the clergy of his diocese, welcoming the I Parliament Bill because "it will add to the wholesome strength of the Upper House (reformed or unreformed)," must have come as a shock to many Tories. But it is evident that Dr. Jayne is animated by no sinister design of " selling the pass." He merely takes the common-sense view of the Arlia- ment Bill to which prejudice has blinded the majority of his party. "Freed from the odium of its Veto," Dr. Jayne argues, the House of Lords " will be able to exercise, on a firmer footing, its statutory rights of criticising, amending, and, within certain limits, of rejecting Bills." Presumably the meaning of the Bishop's last clause is that the delay which the Parliament Bill will allow the Second Chamber to exercise will be quite sufficient to ensure the withdrawal of a measure that has not public opinion behind it. In fact, the Parliament Bill gives the Second Chamber the power of putting on the brake where they used to exercise their " statutory right' by upsetting the train. And to make this simple and salutary change, the Liberal party has had to run the gauntlet of two General elections!
In his great speech on THE GREATEST Saturday Mr. Lloyd ASSET. George dealt with the

difficulty of satisfying the Medical Profession, the difficulty of satisfying the Friendly Societies, and the broader national aspect of his scheme. He addressed reassuring words to both sections, and pointed out to Friendly Society members that they will pay less under the State Insurance scheme and obtain larger benefits than at present. But the main object of the legislative aims embodied in the State Insurance Bill are, as Mr. Lloyd George said, to cultivate in the State a sense of pro- prietorship over the workers, who are the greatest asset of any land. To those who have not yet attained to a clear view of this fundamental position of modern statesman- ship, Mr. Lloyd George would say: "Go to Canada with an offer in one hand of a million of our able-bodied workmen, in the other hand your hundred millions of our sterling gold. Do you think they would hesitate for a moment which to accept? It is the men, .it is the women, they want in order to develop and draw out and increase and improve the wealth and prosperity of their land." •

We hope to make next week's
"Examiner" excel all previous issues in the number and beauty of its illustrations of Coronation events in _ _
Warrington and District. A unique feature will be a large pictorial repro- ..
duction of the Coronation ceremony' in the Abbey, with key-plan to the many notabilities depicted thereon. . .

Warringtonians win) wish to participate " in Coronation festivities on anything like an elaborate and entertaining scale will need to patronise places like Stockton Heath,l Grappenhall, Padgate, and Penketh. They know how to do these things in the villages! * *

Readers of the " Examiner" whose Lotnes may be far away will perhaps not be so interested as their friends here are in the fact that rain fell in Warrington yesterday. Beyond a thunderstorm, and a very slight shower or so, there has been no rain in Warrington and district since the last week in April. At the time of writing, however, umbrellas look like coming into vogue again.

The Tories have foiight the Ross and Cromarty bye-election on Home Rule and pinned their faith to endeavouring to persuade the electors of this scattered constituency that Home Rule means Home Ruin. The poll was declared yesterday, and gave the Liberals a majority of 2,464 in an aggregate of less than 5,000 votes. So much for Redmond and Ruin in Scottish estimation! 0 '_a

Even Mayors must be open to criticism from their lesser townsmen, and we feel bound to express the opinion that his Worship, the Mayor of Warrington, com- mitted an error of judgment when he revived, at the Council meeting, the divute between his committee and the teachers. The result is that the dying embers of resent- ment have been fanned into a flame which may vie with that of the most pretentious Coronation bonfire in the district. Surely, silence would have been golden under the circumstances.

The control of the tramway track has been handed over to the Tramways manager, I with the generous admission on all hands that it is in a disgraceful and dangerous state. We are inclined to sympathise with Mr. Telfer in being saddled with a white elephant while not having the means to keep such an expensive beast. Until the Cor- poration decide boldly to re-lay a big portion of the track, and obtain the money for the purpose, it is little use handing it over to 1 anyone but a collector of antiques and curiosities. _

The Comicil is determined to oppose the carrying out by the County Council of the inadequate scheme for a new bridge at Sankey. Meanwhile Alderman Bolton, in that humorous phraseology of his, wants to know why the committee do not tackle Blackbear Bridge at Latchford, instead of "rambling I about the outskirts of the town." Echo answers, why? Perhaps this hump on the highway to Cheshire will be removed when I the tram-track is re-laid. Ofcourse it should have been done before the tramways appeared at all!

Alderman Bennett in discussing town planning at the Council meeting on Tuesday, made a reference to Stockton Heath whicho we feel sure, will be hailed with acclamation and delight "across the water." Said he: "There was no doubt dat in a few years Stockton Heath would be part of the borough, and surely it was worth while to develop such suburhs on natural, hcalthy lines, so that when the apple was ripe and fell into thiir lap it would be thorough'y sound." Who said: "Urban powers!" • • _

The Mayor has very kindly co-operated with the Bold-street Wesleyan Cripples' Guild, and issued invitations to 100 crippled Warrington children for a motor trip to Chester on the 29th inst., followed by a tea. No one who saw anything of the correspond- ing treat to these poor unfortunate ' youngsters a year ago will feel anything but enthusiasm for the idea. Councillor Bellian is getting together the numerous motor-cars ' required, but he still needs 17 more vehicles, and wishes to appeal to the generosity and , clarity of those fortunate people who possess Imotor-cars and have not yet come to the aid of the scheme.

Tariff Reformers are shy birds when it comes to a question of public debate on the merits of their policy as opposed to Free Trade. Mr. New has placed the local exponents of Tariff Reform in a fix by challenging one of their speakers to a debate. The matter was diplomatically referred to " T.R." headquarters at Manchester, with the result that Mr. New has received an ingenious reply telling him that until the challenge to debate which Mr. Smith issued to Mr. Crosfield some six months ago has been accepted and cleared away, Mr. News challenge must stand over. Mr. New calls this "a weak get out," and we agee with him. But we should very much like to know from our Tariff Reform friends when and where Mr. Smith's valiant challenge was uttered (for we have no recollection of it) and why the matter has been left in abeyance so long?

There is no lack of enthusiasm in the local progressive ranks, and the successful series of open-air meetings held by the Liberal Association and the Progressive Labour League have afforded unmistakable evidence of a healthy spirit and a determination to retrieve Warrington's political reputation at the earliest opportunity. Mr. Lloyd Georges great insurance scheme, which marks the dawn of a brighter era for the workers, formed the chief topic of the addresses at the Bridge Foot meeting on Monday evening and Mr. C. E. Parker and Mr. H. New took the opportunity of removing some misconceptions Mr. Parker's testimony was particularly valuable as coming from an employer, for he maintains that the gain in the health and efficiency of the workers which the scheme will assuredly bring about, will more than counterbalance any additional expenditure to which the masters will be committed.

div.head: Tariff Reformers' Tactics.
div.p: Tariff Reformers' Tactics.

Sir,—May I crave space in your columns for the following On May 15th I was amongst the audience at a Tariff Refotm Meeting at Bridge Foot. The speaker, Mr. Henshall, was making some very disparaging remarks concerning all who held Free Trade views. I remarked that I would gladly debate the (pies- lion with him either in the open air or indoors. He very boldly declared " I am willing to meet may friend, who wants to air his ' knowledge (a cheap sneer) at any time and any place when he likes." Some of the audience natur- ally believed him, no I named the following Thursday. He then, after having a short conversation nith Alderman Bennett, said I most get my name backed by a reaponsible Association, to which I agreed. The next day I wrote to Mr. Dote, who is, I believe, the local secretary. Ile replied with a note far from courteous to myself, no I communicated with the Tariff Reform League at Manchester, who at last have sent the following reply The Tariff Reform League, . . ,
(Lancashire and Cheshire Intsinn). & 34, Corporation ntreat, Manchetrer. June, 1911

Harry New, Esq , Hassey at., Wallington. Dear sir, Further to your letter challenging our Mr. Henshall to debate, I have been making erquiries at Watrington and find that a challenge which Mr. Harold Smith. , made some six months ono le debate with Mr. Crosfield the question of Tariff Reform and Free Trade, Las not yet been accepted. I would suggest *bat if you desire this question to he adequately discussed, it would be better for the leaders of the two parties in Warrington (i.e. Mr. Smith and Mr. Crosfiehl) to debate the matter firet.

I therefore suggest illet the debate between Mr Baseball and yourself stand over until the challenge of Mr. Smith to Mr. thosfield has been accepted, alter which we shall be glad to witting° for the acceptance of your challenge,--Yours faithfully, E. ASHTON Organizing Secretary. . . -

_ Now Air, this is undoubtedly pure bluff —end a very weak "get out of a straighforward challenge. What transpired nix months ego between Mr. Smith and Mr. Crosfield has nothing whatever to do with the cane or myself. I am prepared to meet a loan or men, who I am vain enough to think are no more than my equals, and to drag in two gentlemen and expect them to do what I am quite capable el doing myself is notquite the thing. I hope Tory working men will note how their championa uphold the arguments (sic) they see, and will judge them by their deeds not words. I intend preaching what I nincerely believe to be the with, to most my class and my neighbour. So let cant and hypocracy go we have no room for them and politics will be the cleaner and better.—Very truly yams, HARRY NEW, C 2, Norris-street, Warrington.

The Teachers and the Coronation. Mr. Upson's Reply to the Mayor. Sir,—lour slaw° would not allow of an adequate reply to the attack the Mayor was pleased to make upon me at the Council meeting on faraday last. I can, therefore, only deal with a few poirds. I am amazed that His Worship bas no utterly mis- understood the recent meeting of leachers and I can rely conclude that his arduous duties have not given him sufficient time to read the whole of the proceedings. It was a meeting called to protest against certain charges made against the Teachers at the Education Meeting of May 29tb. A resoluticn repudiating those charges was before the meeting, and JO .OPrOrLing that resolution I said the charges of selfishnese and want of sympathy were hes, and that I am prepared to stand by. Neither I nor any other speaker dreamt of charging the members of the Coronation Sub-committee with untruth- fulness. But the Mayor's indignation SOOMII to he greatest against the CliiiCi•M I ventured to express upon the amount to be spent. Surely more than one cream cf that exists, and the expression of that differenceof opinion ought not to excite to such a degree his Worship's displeasure. I am still untepentent • I still think the amount miserably inadequate. £3OO are take spent on 11,000 children, that is,•6l-7d. per head. (I know a Sunday school where £25 are annually spent on Walking Day on 500 children, that is Is, per Lead.) From this 5 I-7d. is Ito be deducted the cost of the mug. Ido not know 'what that into cost, but I notice many authorities are spending sd. or 6d. on the mug &lore. At any rate I .am given to understand that I d, per head was to lie left for feeding and entertaining the children. The Coronation celebration is to make an indelible impres- sion upon the children's minds. It will. They are to !remember it to the last day of their lives. ' They Ny ill. In old age they are to gather their wondering tad awestruck grandchildren around their knees, while they tell with glowing cheek and kindling eye of the magnificent entertainments, the lavish provision made for them by the City Fathers at the Coronst:on of King George V., and all at a cost of one penny three farthings per head. But why does not the Mayor or Councillor Birtles or any other member of the Coronation Subcomrnittee answer the teachers' objections to their scheme? Mr. Turner gives many in Lis letter. Mr. St...field gam many more is his epeeeb. Yet not a single sttemit haa been made to answer them. Is it denied that Victoria Park is remote from most of the schools ? That the park is partially unfenced from the river ? That there is only one eotrarce ? That it has to be approached by Warrington Bridge? That there are DO mnitary conveniences? No Sir, the objections are unanswerable, the sum to lie spent is an ridiculously small that the Coronation Sub-committee must have realized that the whole thing would le a ghastly failure, and they were glad of MI exert, to drop It. There was something mid of reniot irg difficulties by "give and take." On our nide it was all give. We were prepared to do anything, we volunteered to do anything, even to carry out the first scheme, but—we ventured to enlanit an alternative—there seems to have been our offence—and the whole thing was given up. The Mayor's remark about " going for people, especially when they are not there" is unworthy of him. I was LOL " there," yet he made a among personal attack urn me. Besides be (night to knave me sufficiently well to believe that I will exprese what I feel to be right whether the persons who bold opposite views are there or not.—Yours truly, JOHN UPSON.

Sic,-1 notice in the account of the Council meet- ing, held on Tueeday last, that the Mayor is very indignant at some words which were uttered at the Teachers Protest Meeting. Now, sir, with your permiesicn, I should like to point out that the teachei s of Wart ington were accused of rel6shnesa sad of being unsympathetic towards the children under their charge, because they raisedoljec- lions to, and pointed out the inherent difficulties if a scheme, which to cue, except those from whom it emanated, seems to have • good word for. Cettainly the parents of the children can now see

the absolute impossibility and danger of it. It matters not who made the statements. They were made, and the teachers in v,ew of their put record, as well as t heir present willingness to do all that is pasible for ' the children, were justified in condemning them its , the most forcible and emphatic terms. I notice also, that the Town Clerk said that the teachers refused to help in entertaining the children. Perhaps he had forgotten that the head teachers put forward an alternative scheme, which could have been carried cot much more succesefully, and given infinitely more pleasure to the children, than the one first proposed. div.head: Peace and War.
div.p: Peace and War.

Sir,—ln reply to Mr. ii. S. Townrces almoi( too kind letter on my articles on Mr. Angell'almok entilled " 'the Great Illusion," to some estint agree with the criticism suggestel in Lis two fir*. questions. . _ _

In reference to the first, be suggests that Mr. Agkll 'has placed too much weight on the economic motive for or against war, and eufficieut allowance has not been made for such factors as the ambition of a king, or a ruling caste. There is, however, this to he said— Are not those who are interested in the economic question becaning in all commercial countries, the ruling caste? The ambition of the kings, and the like, is becoming, relatively attenuated, and the economic motive with its relation both to capital and labour becoming the controlling influence. In regard to the second quesion as to the consoli- dation of Germany being establiehed hy the influence of the Franco-German \Var. This is doubtless true, but this was an esceotional result due to circum- stances which would not again be applimble to Oermany, or to any other country that I can think of at the moment.

In reference to the third point which suggetts that in the case of this country being dehated by 201110 rival commercial nation, our factories will close, men will starve, our export trade will stop, and our °vet sea exports will be romplied by other countrice ! This, I take it, is Mr. Townroe'• thought implied in his third gnestion. We will not differ as to the injurious effect upon trade by war. Is fact "The Great Illusion" is written to emphasiee 'bislang. Mr. Townroe appeals to agree that while the cosque, ing nation may not profit directly, it will indirectly. through the inability of the conquered after the war to do an export trade which preen] nedly the emperors would take. I cannot agree with ilr.Tonnroe an this. The conquering country would not hare improved its power of exporting (although it might have increased the necessity of doing so) beeauee of the waste of war which nould only be less than our own. This last, howerei, is doubtful, isa the coat to invaders is gener- ally greater than that of the invaded, because the operations are further from the base. The cyst of the South African war to England was far greater than the cost to the Boers although, England was the conqueror. Mr. Townroe will for- give me if I ask him to recall some very elementary facts in ',said to trade. Ido this because he does not mention imports, but only exprrts, and they ought to be taken in conjunction. Exports by themselves area loss to the count, y, that is, the more we sand out of the products of wraith, the poorer we become unless we take into account what we get in return for the expotte We cop rt only that um may impost. We import those things which minister to human wants, we import that we may gain by the exchange. Bearing this in mind we have primarily to consider what effect war will have upon our impotts. This of course brings in the question of rapine because we attnot expect foreigners to send the things we sent unless Se give them something in return, or do them some aervice for which they have t pip. Errs-Tie ate lien-foie only a means to an end, the trim end being the imports, by Ote help of hich we are ft clothed, and bossed. Probably Mr. Townroe quite recognizes this, but the emphasis he placea upon txporta makes one doubt it. Now let on conceive the situation, as far as exports and imports are concerned, in the case of the defeat of this country by a rival commercial power. We may suppose tha we should have to pay a heavy ind.mnity in some form or other. Let us put its value at a higher figure than ever has been exacted by a conqueror ; any £400,000,0011 We may presume th.it the direct loss to the country ip the waste of matetial, the sinking of our ships, de., to be say £000,000,000; manly • prodigous Adding this to the indemnity we have • material national loss of £1,000,000,000. But the accumu- lated wealth of this rotting is computed to be £11,413,000,000 —the t is the total posaciaione public public and private, of the inhabitants of Great Britain and Ireland. We have therefore a diminution of the known national wealth of nine per cent. Surely Mr Townroe does rot claim that such • lots would result in our factories being closed, our men reduaed to starvation, and our export trade brought. Pia stop? But the point at issue is the possibility of the conquering country securing our export Vlachs through loss and dislocation of trade and credit. ('he reserue would probably be the result. Under normal conditions a country being defeated, and having to pay an indemnity must necessarily pay it in v.:130,aml these goods would smell exports I need not. with Mr. Townroe, go into the (mention of the absurdity of thinking that an indemnity can be paid is c in ma well as measured by it Given a constant yearly figure for investments abioad a defeated country will always increase its exports after a war ; it is natural it should be no. A study of exports if such countries daring the last hundred years wit", I believe, prove this. In view of what I said earlier there is no national benefit in such excess exports beca.e they ere in payment of debts (of which the indemnity f .rtns part) iecarred during the war, ant for which we get nothing in return. It is pert of the price if the folly of going to war, and is the condition of conquer, as well ea conquered, although probably to a smaller extent. But leaving the restate of the rates of exchange, which largely determine the flow of exports end import., it is well to remember that there are other factors constituting the wealth of a country which cannot be touched by war, and although these cannot be expressed in figures, they have a greater effect on the possibilities of trade than accumulated capital. No doubt Mr. Angell bad this in mind when he wrote ' No nation can its our day by military conqueat permanently, or for any considerable period, destroy or greatly damage the trade of another ; since trade depends upon the existence of natural wealth, and • population capable of working it." The true potential wealth of any muntry is in the country itself and the skill of the workers, and the diminution of a percentage of the accumu- lated capital would be of minor importance as long as the factors mentioned remain. There is no wealth producer comparable to the human mind ;no known generating force so powerful as brain cells, directing the still of hand, and controlling, and making subservient,nature's forces and material. Here is the latent power which can quickly replace capital, and I agree with Mr. Angell that so long as the natural wealth of the country and the population to work it remains, no long an the sun shines upon England, as long as her agricultural and mineral wealth remain unaffected,aud CBlloot be paid away as part of the indemnity, it in impossiole for any country to greatly damage the trade of another and to appropriate that trade to itself. There is the further point which Mr. Angell puts forward " To whatever extent a cooqueret cam destroy the trade of the conquered; to that erect he is destroying his cern market, actual or potential." T. urn, etc., CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, Rum 13th, 1911.

It used to be thought that only urinary troubles and backache were to be traced to the kidneys, but modern science now shows that many fatal diseases have their beginning in irregularities of these important organs.

For the kidneys are the blood purifiers. Every few minutes the blood passes through them to be purified. When it reaches the kidneys it is heavily laden with uric acid and liquid waste—when it leaves the kidneys its impurities have been taken out just as if it had passed through a filter.

But when the kidneys are weak and inflamed they cannot keep up with their great work, and so the poisonous waste is left in the blood, and the whole body is being slowly poisoned. You soon feel languid, dizzy, and worn out. You cannot sleep—cannot eat--you grow irritable and miserable.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. F. G. BENNETT.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. F. G. BENNETT.

Many of our reader, will deeply regret to hear of the death of Mr. Fredetick Garnett Bennett, who passed away at his residence 133, Lovely-lane, shortly after hue old!, dr on Saturday afternoon. For some months the deceased gentleman had been in a delicate state of health owing to a throat affect it n,and the end, although it came somewhat suddenly, was not unexpected. Mr. Bennett, who wan the second son of the late Mr. William Garnett Bennett, of Manchester, was born on August 11th, 1861. His father will Ire, remembered by the older generation of Warring- milieu, for many years ago he WAS connected with Messrs. Cartwright, Bank Quay, one of the oldrat firms of glans manufacturrie in the country. Subsequently lie entered into business on his own account in Manchester. The Ide Mr. F. G. Bennett received his education at Trent College, near Nottingham, arid gained ilia early commercial expel- ends with hi, father, afterwards entering the servic e of Messrs. Cannington, Shaw, at.d Co., Ltd„ Si, Helens. His conscientious attention to duty and never failing kindlineas gained B. confidence and respect of employers and employed, by whom lie will be greatly missed. For the put eleven yea's he had acted as secretary of the company. Although his busineas associations were with St He'ens, Mr. Bennett had made War, iegton his home for the pant thirty yea! s. At cne time he lived at Fairfield Bank, Manchester-road, with his great aunt, , the lute Miss Garnett, and it is nineteen years since he took op his residence at 133, Lovely-lane, the house having then been newly-erected. Ile was a staunch Churchman and was much dented to St.l'aul's Church,nf a Melt he was one of the oldest sidesmen. Ile wan for many years a member of the Conservative Club:and was also a Freemason, being associated w ith the Lodge of Lights, the Ella. Ashtnole Chapter and the St. Austin's Mark Lodge. Ile was of a generous disposition aid did much good ins quiet way,w hile his taniality and sympathetic manner had gained for him the esteem of a large circle of friotids.

div.head: THE.PRINCE OFIIWALES.
div.p: THE.PRINCE OFIIWALES.

Greece. It MIS • very pipissant tame, warn plenty of fun, some amount of roughing it, and abundant opportun it ies for gaining knowledge of men and countries. On return- ing to England, Prince Albert Victor pro- ceeded to Cambridge, while Prince George continued his naval studies.

In 1889 the Prinoe was presented with his first comma's& that of torpedo boat No. 79. for the period of the naval manieuvres. A year later he commissioned the fi rst-elaee gunboat Thrush, and in her he spent a year on the North American Station, visiting Canada and Jamaica. Ships of the Thrush pleas do not carry a naval chaplain, us Prinoe George, as captain, had to read morning prayers each day and conduct the Sunday service. His favourite hymns were "Nearer, my God. to Thee," and "0 God, our help in ages past."

Horse-racing Ilan only of recent years begun to interest him, lie is • fair hand at billiards, plays golf, and in his younger days was a promising boxer; and cricket, polo, football, and hockey owe a heavy debt to his patronage.

div.head: HEIR TO THE THRONE.
div.p: HEIR TO THE THRONE.

In January, 1892, the whole course of the Prinoe's career w. changed by the death of hie brother, the Duke of Clarence, and he became Duke of York and heir to the throne of England. On July 6, 181t3, the Duke was married at the Chapel Royal, St. James's, to his cousin, Princess Victoria Mary ("May"), the only daughter of the Duke and Duchees of 'Peck. The engagement was immensely popular throughout the Empire, which in many ways showed its approval of the fact that a .ining English King had taken a bonnie English girl for his wife. The Duke and his father, then Prinoe of Wales, were to dine with the Benchers of the Middle Temple one evening, but only the father turned up. As he said in his epeech, apologising for his eon's absence. "A young man who has only been engaged to a charming young lady for two days must be forgiven for wishing to be with her."

div.head: All IMPERIAL MISSION.
div.p: All IMPERIAL MISSION.

In the year following the death of Queen Victoria the new King. an Duke of Cornwall and York, undertook the great Imperial ohm- lion through which he ie chiefly known to his subjects in the Overman Dominions of the Crown. On March 7 the Duke and Duchene bade farewell to their ehildreu and sailed in the Ophir for the East. King Edward's bust words to them, "Make your minds easy, and we will look after the children," illuetrated very well the affection which existed between kin Majesty and his son's family. Their route took them by way of Gibraltar, Malta. l'ort Said, and Colombo, to Adelaide, Sydney, Brieballf, and Melbourne. Subsequently the tour was extended to include New Zealand, South Africa, and Canada. On May 9 the Com- monwealth Parliament of Australia was opened with great ceremony by the Duke of loft, in the presence of 12,000 epectators. Many of the Dutch inhabitants of Cal. Colony took part in the cordial reception given to them, anti there was a great gather- ing of native chiefs who had come to offer their homage to the heir to the British throne.

div.p: OUR ENGLISH QUEEN. A Noble Wife and Mother. AN ENTHUSIASTIC PATRIOT.

Ring George's Queen is the first Engl ieh- woman publicly chosen for wife by an Eng- lish heir-apparent since Edward the Black Prince married the Fair Maid of Kent. 'I he Queen's birth on May 26, 1867, was attended b• the happy omen that it took place in Kensington Palace, the old London palace which had witnessed that of Queen Victoria. and, with the exception of a brief sojourn in Itoly Her Majesty's childhood and youth were entirely epent in this country. Warm-hearted and overflowing with eym- pathy as win, the Duch,. of 'leek, I er Majesty's mother, she had strict - rha pe old-fashioned- -notion, concerning education. She once wrote to an intimate friend, "A , child has quite enough to do to learn obedience and to attend to her lemons, and to grow without many parties and late hours, which take the I reshness of childhood away, and the brigh t nem and beauty Irom girlhood." The governemes of the young Princes. were asked to take particular care to train their royal charge in habits of order and regularity. QUEEN VICTORIA'S FAVOURITE The little Princess was a great favourite with Queen Victoria. There is • pretty little More told which well illustrates " May's, " loyalty to her Sovereign. Geo- graphy was one of her pet subjects, and one day As was set to do an outline map of the in-rid from memory. "Why, you have left out China!" said her governess when the map was presented for her inspection.. " Don't you know where it is?" ^Yes, I know quite well where it ehould be, but I am not going to put it in my map. The Queen is angry with Chion just now, and it has no right to have a place in the world at all ! " was the unexpected reply. The future Queen's favourite authors, even when she was quite a young girl, were George Eliot and Carlyle. In those days she showed herself a very unaffected, simple- minded girl. with a strong sense of 'management," which was divided among charities and hounehold matters. She and her mother became managers of an impor- tant branch of the Ladies' Needlework Guild, and the young Princeae devoted many hours with the membere of the Children's Happy Evenings Association.

div.head: VISITS TO INDIA AND CANADA.
div.p: VISITS TO INDIA AND CANADA.

In 1906 the Prince, with the Prir.coes of Wok" vinited India. Within the space of four and • half months, they saw more of India than most people are privileged to see in a lifetime, and everywhere they left an impression of gracious and kindly in the welfare of. the mutilation.

Princess navy serge and white drill sailor suits for the boys, navy serge skirts and white sailor blouses for the little Princess. , Princeas Mary's education has naturally been the object of the Queen's special solici- tude. She determined that her little daugh. ter should grow up a domesticated woman as well as an accomplished one. As a tiny girl Princess Mary was taught to new by her mother, and one of her duties was to assist in darning her brothers' /Jocks. Cooking in. struction came next, and Princess Mary, provided with her own little pasteboard, rolling-pin, and pots and pans, made splen- did progress in the culinary art. Sincere an is her Majesty's interest in everything concerning Greater Britain, she felt with terrible intensity the parting and the long separation from her children which her tours of our Colonial Empire involved. _ .

Beyond a gift for languars, and a native quickness of reception, the Queen is not a brilliant woman. But ehe bring.; up her children with a high sense of honour. obedi• ence. and duty to their station. Her little daughter is very clever, but every tendency to "Allow off" is repressed. In this the Queen in aided by the King, who haa a word in every detail of hie children'. up-bringing.

div.head: PATRIOT OF PATRIOTS.
div.p: A PATRIOT OF PATRIOTS.

The Queen is a patriot of patriots, and never, if she knows it, wears a yard of material that is not of British manufacture. In 1893, when her engagement was announced, she gave an enormous fillip to home industries by her decree that the Royal trousseau shouA be entirely of British workmanship. "All the silk shall come from England, 11:1 the Ilannel from Wales, all the tweeds from Scotland, and every yard of lace and poplin from Ireland," she declared.

The people reply, the trumpets sound, and the Bible, paten, and chalioe are placed on the altar. The various articles of the Regalia are also placed there. The Litany in sung by two Bishops, the Communion Service is begun, and the Bishop of London preaches a short sermon, aft, which the King, hitherto imcovered, puts on his cap of crimson velvet, turned up with ermine. CORONATION Msom....—The children of Orford School had. very pleasant surprise on Monday, when they were each one given a coronation medal. Mr. klailwood, one of the managers, gave the medals, and his wife and daughter presented them to the children. The medal is a handsome brass one.
